messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Target: $V_{out\_min} \ge 4.5\text{V}$, $V_{out\_max} \le 5.5\text{V}$, ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$, startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, settled $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20M$\Omega$).
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude (S1): $\approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   The Reference Design (FBR - Full Bridge Rectifier) failed because $V_{oc} = 3.8\text{V}$ is too low to reach the required 4.5V-5.5V range given diode drops and the load.
    *   Constraint: Need a DC-DC step-up mechanism. Since it's a piezo energy harvester, a common high-efficiency approach is SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or a simple boost converter/charge pump.

    *   $V_{oc}$ is around 3.8V. To reach 4.5V-5.5V, we need a voltage gain.
    *   Standard FBR is passive and cannot provide gain (only rectification).
    *   SSHI uses an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement/voltage, effectively increasing the voltage available for rectification.
    *   Specifically, Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI) or Series-SSHI (S-SSHI).
    *   The provided `SYNC` controller is ideal for SSHI. It closes switches at the piezo voltage extrema (zero crossings of current).

    *   *Option 1: SSHI (Parallel)*
        - $C_p$ is in parallel with the source.
        - An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ are used to invert $V_{C_p}$.
        - The inverted voltage adds to the source voltage, pushing it above the diode threshold and the target $V_{out}$.
        - Components: Rectifier (FBR or Half-Bridge) + Inductor + Switch + Sync.

    *   *Option 2: Charge Pump (Dickson/Cross-coupled)*
        - Hard to implement with just a `SYNC` and basic components without a clock. `SYNC` tracks frequency, so it's basically a clock.
        - However, SSHI is generally more efficient for piezo.

    *   *Option 3: Boost Converter (Synchronous/Non-synchronous)*
        - Usually requires a more complex controller than the provided `SYNC`. The `SYNC` closes for a short `ton` at extrema. This is exactly what's needed for inductor-based inversion in SSHI.

    *   Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   We want to invert the charge on $C_p$.
    *   Let's try a simplified SSHI structure:
        - Rectifier to charge $C_{out}$.
        - Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with $C_p$ to flip voltage.
        - Wait, the standard P-SSHI involves flipping the voltage across $C_p$ *before* it's rectified.
        - Architecture:
            1.  Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
            2.  A rectifier (Full Bridge) connected to `pzp`/`pzn` and `out`.
            3.  An inversion circuit: Inductor $L$ from `pzp` to a node `n1`, Switch $S$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
            4.  `SYNC` controller `G1` controls `S`.
            5.  `G1` closes at `edges: both` (every half cycle).
            6.  `ton` $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{mH}$, $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 15\mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Refining the Rectifier:*
        A full bridge (4 diodes) might have too much drop (0.5V x 2 = 1V). A half-bridge (2 diodes) might be better if we can use the `pzn` as a reference, but `pzn` is part of the AC source. Actually, if we use a full bridge, the output is $V_{out} = V_{pzp-pzn} - 2 V_d$. If $V_{oc}$ is 3.8V, $V_{out}$ max is $\approx 3.3\text{V}$, which explains the FBR failure.
        With SSHI, the effective $V_{pzp-pzn}$ increases.

    *   *Alternative: Synchronous Rectification (using switches):*
        The `SYNC` controller can only control 4 switches total. If we use 2 for rectification, we have 2 left for inversion.
        But a simple diode bridge is more robust for a first try if the inversion gain is enough.

    *   *Design 1: P-SSHI with Full Bridge (FBR)*
        - Rectifier: 4x DSCH (Standard FBR).
        - Inversion: $L_1$ (`pzp` $\to$ `n1`), $S_1$ (`n1` $\to$ `pzn`), `G1` (SYNC, `edges: both`).
        - Storage: $C_{out}$ (`out` $\to$ `0`).

    *   *Design 2: P-SSHI with Half Bridge (if possible)*
        - Some piezo designs use a single diode and a capacitor. But we need a stable DC output.
        - Let's try a "Synchronous" rectification if we can. But the `SYNC` is designed for inversion.
        - Let's try a different inversion topology: a "voltage doubler" approach? No, SSHI is the standard.

    *   *Design 3: SSHI with a Zener clamp?*
        - The target is 4.5V to 5.5V. A Zener `DZ33` is 3.3V, which is too low. It would clamp the output to 3.3V. We don't need it if the storage capacitor and load regulate the voltage, or if we use a higher value Zener (not available). We only have `DZ33`. So we avoid it unless we are overshooting.

    *   $S1$: $I_p = 60\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=2.2\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   $P_{load} = V^2 / R_L \approx 4.5^2 / 2.2\text{M} \approx 9.2\mu\text{W}$.
    *   $P_{avail} \approx 0.5 \cdot C_p \cdot V_{oc}^2 \cdot f \approx 0.5 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot 3.8^2 \cdot 100 \approx 18\mu\text{W}$.
    *   The power budget is tight but feasible.

    *   Wait, is there a better way to use the `SYNC` controller?
        If we use a synchronous rectifier (switches instead of diodes), we eliminate the $2 \times 0.25\text{V}$ drop.
        - $S_1$ (`pzp` $\to$ `out`), $S_2$ (`pzn` $\to$ `out`) - This doesn't make sense for a rectifier.
        - A bridge would need 4 switches. We only have 4 switches total.
        - If we use 4 switches for the bridge, we have none for inversion.
        - If we use 2 diodes and 2 switches?

    *   Let's stick to the P-SSHI (FBR + L-S inversion). It's the most standard approach to boost piezo voltage.

    *   *Topology 1 (P-SSHI):*
        - D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        - D2: `pzn` -> `out` (Wait, FBR is: `pzp`->`out`, `pzn`->`out`, `0`->`pzp`, `0`->`pzn`? No, that's not right. Standard FBR: `pzp` -> `out` (D1), `pzn` -> `out` (D2), `0` -> `pzp` (D3), `0` -> `pzn` (D4). No, that's a mistake.
        Correct FBR:
        - Diode 1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
        - Diode 2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
        - Diode 3: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (Incorrect: should be `pzp` $\to$ `0` when `pzn` is positive)
        Wait, the correct bridge is:
        - `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1)
        - `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2)
        - `pzp` $\to$ `0` (D3)
        - `pzn` $\to$ `0` (D4)
        Let's trace:
        When $V_{pzp} > V_{pzn}$: $D1$ is on (`pzp` $\to$ `out`), $D4$ is on (`pzn` $\to$ `0`).
        When $V_{pzn} > V_{pzp}$: $D2$ is on (`pzn` $\to$ `out`), $D3$ is on (`pzp` $\to$ `0`).
        This is the standard full-bridge rectifier.

    *   *Refining Topology 1:*
        - Components:
            - D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
            - D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
            - D3: `pzp`, `0` (DSCH)
            - D4: `pzn`, `0` (DSCH)
            - L1: `pzp`, `n1`
            - S1: `n1`, `pzn`
            - G1: SYNC (ton: 20e-6, phase: 0, edges: "both")
            - C1: `out`, `0`

    *   *Wait, does the SYNC controller close at the right time for this?*
        "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
        At the voltage extrema, the current is zero. This is exactly when you want to flip the voltage in SSHI.
        For P-SSHI, you flip the voltage at the peak of the cycle.
        If the voltage is $V_{max}$, you flip it to $-V_{max}$. Then the source continues to push it towards $+V_{max}$, meaning the voltage across the piezo becomes $2 V_{max}$. This significantly increases the voltage available to the rectifier.

    *   *Let's try a second topology: SSHI with a different rectifier?*
        Maybe a half-bridge if we center the piezo?
        - Piezo `pzp` and `pzn`.
        - C_mid from `pzn` to `0`? No.
        - Let's try a "Charge Pump" style. But the `SYNC` is so perfectly suited for SSHI.

    *   *Wait, let's check the components again.*
        Max 16 components.
        Topology 1: 4 diodes, 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC, 1 capacitor = 8 components. Plenty of room.

    *   *Check the phase and edges:*
        `edges: "both"` means it triggers at both the positive and negative peaks of the voltage (where current is zero). This is correct for SSHI.
        `phase`: 0 is the default. A small shift might be needed to ensure the switch closes *after* the peak. Let's try 0.0 first.

    *   *One more thing: the value of L and C.*
        $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
        For $L = 10\text{mH}$, $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC_p} = 1/\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = 1/\sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 63245 \text{ rad/s}$.
        $t_{on} \approx \pi / \omega_0 = \pi \cdot \sqrt{L C_p} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        Let's set $L=10\text{mH}$ and $t_{on}=50\mu\text{s}$ as a starting point.

    *   *Topology 2: Parallel SSHI with a "Synchronous Rectifier" using switches.*
        Since we have 4 switches, we could potentially use 2 for the bridge (half-wave) and 2 for inversion.
        But diode bridges are safer. Let's try another inversion method.
        What if we use a "voltage doubler" (Greinacher circuit)?
        It uses 2 diodes and 2 capacitors.
        - C1 from `pzp` to `n1`
        - D1 from `n1` to `0`
        - C2 from `n1` to `out`
        - D2 from `pzp` to `out`
        This is essentially a step-up. But it's not as efficient as SSHI for piezo.

    *   *Topology 3: SEH (Synchronous Electric Harvesting) - essentially SSHI.*
        Wait, the provided reference design used a 2.2uF capacitor. Let's use a similar value for $C_{out}$.

    *   P-SSHI (Inductor-Switch inversion) + Full Bridge (4x DSCH).
    *   This is the most likely candidate to boost 3.8V to 5V.

    *   `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1)
    *   `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2)
    *   `pzp` $\to$ `0` (D3)
    *   `pzn` $\to$ `0` (D4)
    *   `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (L1)
    *   `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (S1)
    *   `S1` controlled by `G1` (SYNC)
    *   `out` $\to$ `0` (C1)

    Wait, the `S` component: `nodes: [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC`.
    L1 is in series with S1. So L1 is from `pzp` to `n1`, and S1 is from `n1` to `pzn`. This creates a loop `pzp` $\to$ `n1` $\to$ `pzn` $\to$ `pzp` when S1 is closed.

    - S1: nominal; $I_p=60\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=2.2\text{M}\Omega$
    - S2: heavy load; $R_L=1\text{M}\Omega$
    - S3: strong excitation; $I_p=120\mu\text{A}, R_L=10\text{M}\Omega$
    - S4: weak excitation; $I_p=40\mu\text{A}, R_L=4.7\text{M}\Omega$
    - S5: low frequency; $f=80\text{Hz}, R_L=3.3\text{M}\Omega$
    - S6: $C_p=30\text{nF}, R_L=2.2\text{M}\Omega$

    The SSHI circuit should handle these. The $t_{on}$ will be tuned by the evolution strategy.

    *   Diodes: `DSCH` (lowest drop).
    *   L: 10mH (starting value).
    *   C: 2.2uF (starting value).
    *   S: controlled by G1.
    *   G1: `edges: "both"`, `ton: 50e-6`, `phase: 0.0`.

    Is there any other way to boost? A charge pump using the SYNC switches?
    - S1: `pzp` to `n1`
    - S2: `n1` to `out`
    This would be a switched-capacitor boost. But the `SYNC` pulses are very short (`ton` up to 1ms), which is better for LC resonance than for charging large capacitors.

    Let's stick with P-SSHI as the primary. I'll propose a slightly different variation as a second option, maybe a half-bridge rectifier to reduce diode drops?
    Half-Bridge SSHI:
    - Piezo `pzp` and `pzn`.
    - $S_1$ and $L_1$ for inversion (same as P-SSHI).
    - Rectifier: One diode $D_1$ from `pzp` to `out`, and $C_{bias}$ from `pzn` to `0`? No, the piezo is a current source, so $V_{pzn}$ will float.
    Actually, if we use a half-bridge:
    - $D_1$ from `pzp` to `out`.
    - $C_1$ from `pzn` to `0`.
    But the piezo current source is between `pzp` and `pzn`. If we put $C_1$ from `pzn` to `0`, the current will charge $C_1$. This is basically a center-tapped transformer approach. Not ideal.

    What about a "Voltage Doubler" (Charge Pump) using the SYNC switches?
    - S1: `pzp` to `n1`
    - S2: `n1` to `out`
    - S3: `pzn` to `n2`
    - S4: `n2` to `out`
    This could work, but `ton` is very small.

    Let's try two P-SSHI variants.
    Variant 1: Full bridge.
    Variant 2: Full bridge but with a different inversion path (e.g., L and S in a different configuration). No, the standard P-SSHI is most robust.

    Actually, let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" (using switches instead of diodes) to see if that helps with the voltage.
    If we use 2 switches for rectification and 2 for inversion?
    - S1: `pzp` to `out` (closed when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$)
    - S2: `pzn` to `out` (closed when $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$)
    - S3: `pzp` to `n1`
    - S4: `n1` to `pzn`
    Wait, the `SYNC` controller pulses are based on the *piezo voltage extrema*. Rectification needs to happen *during* the cycle, not just at the extrema.
    - Extrema: current = 0.
    - Rectification: current is flowing.
    So the `SYNC` controller is *only* useful for the inversion switch, not for the rectifier switches.

    Conclusion: Use diode bridge for rectification and `SYNC` for the SSHI inversion.

    One more check on the full bridge nodes:
    D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
    D3: `pzp` $\to$ `0`
    D4: `pzn` $\to$ `0`
    Wait, this is the same as:
    D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
    D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (This is wrong, diodes are [anode, cathode])
    Correct:
    - D1: `pzp`, `out`
    - D2: `pzn`, `out`
    - D3: `0`, `pzp` (No, this would conduct when `pzp` is negative)
    Let's re-verify.
    Full bridge:
    - Node A (`pzp`), Node B (`pzn`).
    - Path 1: A $\to$ D1 $\to$ `out`
    - Path 2: B $\to$ D2 $\to$ `out`
    - Path 3: A $\to$ D3 $\to$ `0`
    - Path 4: B $\to$ D4 $\to$ `0`
    When $V_A > V_B$:
    - Current flows $A \to D1 \to \text{out} \to \text{load} \to 0 \to D4 \to B$.
    - So D1 (`pzp`, `out`) and D4 (`0`, `pzn`) are on.
    Wait, D4 anode is `0`, cathode is `pzn`. This is correct.
    When $V_B > V_A$:
    - Current flows $B \to D2 \to \text{out} \to \text{load} \to 0 \to D3 \to A$.
    - So D2 (`pzn`, `out`) and D3 (`0`, `pzp`) are on.
    Correct Bridge:
    - D1: `pzp`, `out`
    - D2: `pzn`, `out`
    - D3: `0`, `pzp`
    - D4: `0`, `pzn`

    Let's double check:
    D1: anode=`pzp`, cathode=`out`
    D2: anode=`pzn`, cathode=`out`
    D3: anode=`0`, cathode=`pzp`
    D4: anode=`0`, cathode=`pzn`
    Yes, this is a standard full-bridge rectifier.

    - Structure: P-SSHI
    - Components: 4 Diodes (DSCH), 1 Inductor, 1 Switch, 1 SYNC, 1 Capacitor.
    - L1 value: 10mH.
    - C1 value: 2.2uF.
    - G1: ton=50e-6, phase=0, edges="both".
    - RL is handled by the test bench.
    - Power cost of SYNC is handled by the test bench.

    Could we use a Zener for protection? $V_{out\_max} = 5.5\text{V}$. The `DZ33` zener clamps at 3.3V, which is too low. We don't need it.

    What if we use a different inversion topology?
    The "S-SSHI" (Series SSHI) puts the inductor in series with the piezo.
    S-SSHI:
    - Piezo `pzp` $\to$ L1 $\to$ `n1`.
    - S1 from `n1` to `pzn`.
    - Rectifier from `n1` and `pzn`.
    P-SSHI is generally more common and easier to implement.
